title: Routes, transit times and the exposure window

the_number_that_matters.finding: A ship is inside the Gulf of Aden danger corridor for roughly 33 to 49 hours. The Internationally Recommended Transit Corridor is about 490 nautical miles long and 2 nautical miles wide, as two one-mile lanes.
the_number_that_matters.why_it_matters: This is the mission length an escort has to cover. It is a bounded, well-defined corridor with published traffic lanes, not open ocean. Any platform that can hold merchant speed for two days covers it.
the_number_that_matters.caveat: The hours are arithmetic on the published 490 nm length, not a published figure. They exclude manoeuvring, weather and traffic.

irtc.lanes: two one-mile lanes, one each direction
irtc.reporting: Vessels register with MSCHOA and report to UKMTO. Naval coordination is organised around the corridor. BMP does not specify a permanent scheduled convoy timetable.

suez.value: SDR per Suez Canal Net Tonnage band, varying by vessel type. No single flat rate.

panama.metric: Slot auction, one additional transit, LNG carrier

cape_diversion.value: up to 40% more for a journey

gaps: No Cape-route distances retrieved, so the Suez comparison cannot be computed from our own figures.
No transit times in days for any named route.
No representative Suez or Panama toll in dollars for a specific vessel. Both authorities publish calculators, not headline prices.
No length or exposure time for the Bab el-Mandeb and southern Red Sea segment, which is where the Houthi attacks happen. We have the Gulf of Aden corridor only.
The extra Cape fuel is published as a percentage, never in tonnes or dollars for a stated vessel.
